1:
Whether David wrote this psalm is disputed inside the catena, and in one place inside a single block. Adam Clarke sets the title against the language: notwithstanding the Hebrew inscription and the versions that follow it, there is internal evidence that the psalm was not written by David but during or after the captivity, since several Chaldaisms occur in it, which he collates with passages in Daniel. The composition is worthy of David, he grants, but the language appears to be lower than his time, and the author is unknown. Keil and Delitzsch reach much the same conclusion by a milder route: the psalm is inscribed to David only because it is composed after the Davidic model, a counterpart to his didactic psalms, though in contents and poetic character it is in every way worthy of him. Charles Ellicott supports the case at the level of detail, calling one word an Aramaic form found nowhere else and another an Aramaic expression. John Calvin, who assumes David throughout, is followed by a paragraph reporting the whole quarrel and naming Clarke in it, and then answering with a critic who cannot understand how anyone could assign the psalm to another, since the two Chaldaisms consist merely in the substitution of one letter for another very like it in shape, easily mistaken by a transcriber used to the Chaldee idiom.

The verb rendered compassest divides them further. Clarke translates it thou dost winnow, ventilate, or sift my path. Matthew Henry takes that sense morally: God sifts our path so as thoroughly to distinguish between the good and evil of what we do, as by sifting we separate between the corn and the chaff. Calvin agrees the word means to winnow and that the common rendering gives the meaning though not the precise idea, and canvasses the alternatives at length, noting the Septuagint’s thou hast investigated, one bishop’s supposition that the metaphor is taken from hunting, and an archbishop’s complaint that winnowing would sound uncouth. Ellicott finds real obscurity: the Hebrew first means to scatter, used of throwing corn about; Theodotion and the Latin have traced or investigated, Jerome winnowed, while the received rendering appears to come from a mistaken etymology. His own preference abandons the figure for a verb meaning to lodge, which makes a perfect parallel with the next clause — about my path and bed thou art a guest, in all my ways thou dwellest. John Wesley keeps a third image altogether, a metaphor from soldiers besieging their enemies and setting watches round about them.

A like split follows. John Gill reports that two commentators, father and son, render the next word thou hast formed me and interpret it of the formation of the body, but he keeps besetting, since God compasses men with his presence and providence so that nothing escapes. Clarke adopts the other, following an emendation that unites two verses so the sense runs, thou hast formed me, and laid thy hand upon me. Ellicott reads beset as of a beleaguered city from which there is no escape; Henry hears in the laid hand an allusion to the physician laying his hand upon his patient to feel how the pulse beats. C.H. Spurgeon presses the searching figure hard, as officers search a man for contraband goods or as pillagers ransack a house for plunder, then pulls back, warning that searching ordinarily implies a measure of ignorance removed by observation, which is not the case here. Augustine of Hippo hears the whole under another speaker: Christ speaks in the prophets sometimes in his own name and sometimes in ours, so that what is said in the person of the flesh he took belongs both to the head already ascended and to the members still toiling.
7:
What the spirit named here is gets three answers. John Gill canvasses them in order: some interpret the word literally of the wind, which God brings out of his treasures and which blows everywhere; rather God himself is meant, who is a Spirit, simple and uncompounded, yet unlike all other spirits in being uncreated and immense; or it may signify his all-conscious mind; though it seems best of all, Gill concludes, to understand it of the third Person. Adam Clarke forecloses the first option flatly: the word must here be taken personally, it certainly cannot mean either breath or wind, and to render it so would make the passage ridiculous. He then presses the second clause, which is literally from thy faces, and asks why the plural is used of God and why spirit and faces stand together in one verse; a Trinitarian would at once say the plurality of persons in the Godhead is intended, and who can prove that he is mistaken? Charles Ellicott reads the same clause developmentally: taken alone it would mean no more than creative and providential power, but set in parallel with presence it leads on to a thought the older theology was dimly feeling after and which found its perfect expression in the words spoken to the woman of Samaria.

The flights themselves are read as a compass. John Wesley makes the second pair a flight from east to west, the sea being the western border of Canaan and so often put for the west. Ellicott agrees and admires: the image suggests not only the pinions of cloud that seem to lift the dawn into the sky but the swift sailing of the light across the world, and the poet imagines himself darting from east to farthest west with the rapidity of light. On the descent, Ellicott finds a real advance of thought, since the conviction that the underworld is not exempt from the vigilance and even the visitation of God stands against earlier psalms where death cuts a man off altogether. Clarke distributes the presence by attribute — in heaven in glory, below in vindictive justice, everywhere else by omnipresence. C.H. Spurgeon notices that no answer comes: the reply to the first question is its echo, a second one, and we are as near to God as our soul is to our body, so that we offend him to his face and commit acts of treason at the very foot of his throne.

The darkness verse divides them. Gill and Clarke take it plainly, of a man supposing the night will screen what he does. Ellicott proposes a bolder rendering, let darkness crush me, and light become night around me, observing that commentators have mostly been frightened by that metaphor although the older versions preserved it and Latin writers could speak in prose of a region oppressed by darkness. Then he argues himself back: since the main thought is that there is no escape in height or depth or distance, we seem after all to need darkness. Clarke, having said that God is all sight, all hearing, all feeling, and that his essence is unimpartible while his influence is diffusible, breaks off into open polemic against those who would make the fountain of eternal love a streamlet of capricious love to thousands and a tide of hatred to millions. Matthew Henry keeps the argument tidy: if God is omnipresent he must needs be omniscient. Keil and Delitzsch mark the turn, that what has been said of man being manifest in every place is now confirmed from the origin of man.
13:
One figure dominates this section, and three of them work it out together. Adam Clarke reports a bishop who takes the two words of the fifteenth verse to describe the two principal parts of the body, the bony skeleton that is the foundation of the whole and the external covering of muscular flesh, tendons, veins, arteries, nerves and skin, a curious web of fibres; and he quotes at length another who calls the metaphor one drawn from the nicest tapestry work, rendering it, when I was wrought, as with a needle, in the lowest parts of the earth. That second writer adds the point that gives the figure its weight: the most artful embroidery with the needle was dedicated by the Hebrews to the service of the sanctuary, prescribed by law for a part of the high priest’s dress and for the curtains of the tabernacle, so that the divine workmanship on the body is compared with the finest work men made for God. Clarke then quotes a third hand carrying the image forward, that as an embroiderer keeps his pattern before him, so from the rude skeins of variously coloured silk or worsted there at length arises an unexpected beauty and an accurate harmony of colours and proportions. Charles Ellicott confirms the figure from the same tabernacle passages but leaves it open whether the work is weaving or embroidery.

On the word for the unformed thing they converge unusually. Keil and Delitzsch derive it from a root meaning to roll or wrap together and note that in the Talmud it is used of any unshapen mass or raw material, the wood or metal that is to be formed into a vessel. John Gill calls it a bottom of yarn wound up, Clarke an indistinct mass wrapped up together before it was unfolded into the lineaments of man, Ellicott a word used elsewhere of a mantle and of bales. But the verse that follows divides them sharply. Clarke keeps the received reading, in which the members were written in the book, and builds on it; Ellicott holds that inserting the word members yields a possible but not a probable interpretation, refers the pronoun instead to the days, and after setting out two renderings prefers a slight change giving, the days which are all reckoned, and not one of them is wanting. He also rejects outright the suggestion that the rolled thing is the ball of the threads of destiny, on the ground that this is not a Hebrew conception.

The word fearfully is read two ways. Clarke takes it of frailty: the texture of the body is so exquisitely nice and delicate that the slightest accident may destroy in a moment some part essential to the continuance of life, and God has made us so to teach us to walk with death, keeping life in view. Ellicott renders it fearfully separated or distinguished, which might mean separated from the womb, that is, born, or, if the reference is national rather than individual, the choice of one nation in distinction from other races. Gill answers the numbering of the sand with a run of ancient authorities, and C.H. Spurgeon says God is as much at home in a man’s inmost parts as a landlord on his own estate. On the last clause Clarke reads plain protection night and day, while Ellicott hears dreams continued into the early thoughts of waking. Matthew Henry orders the whole under three heads, that the divine counsels are precious, numerous and constant. John Wesley reads the book as the counsel and providence by which the work was contrived and effected.
19:
Whether these verses belong to the psalm at all is the first question. Adam Clarke denies it: the remaining part has no visible connection with what precedes, and he rather thinks it a fragment, or a part of some other psalm. Charles Ellicott grants the abruptness and then explains it. Such a transition, from a theme so profound and fascinating to fierce indignation against the enemies of God, would certainly be strange anywhere but in the Psalms; yet the subject of omniscience must philosophically conduct the mind to the thought of the existence of evil. The difference is one of temper: the Hebrew never speculated for speculation’s sake, the practical concerns of life engaging him too intensely, and where a modern would have branched off into the recurring problem of how evil entered the world, the Israelite turned with indignation on those who then and there proved the existence of sin in concrete act. Keil and Delitzsch supply the same hinge in one exclamation, that this God is by many not only not believed in and loved but even hated and blasphemed, so that the poet now turns toward these enemies in profound vexation of spirit. C.H. Spurgeon makes the inference from the earlier part directly: crimes committed before the face of the judge are not likely to go unpunished, and God who sees all evil will slay all evil.

The following verse defeats them. Clarke reports a bishop’s rendering, that they have deserted him who are disobedient to God, and men sworn to a rash purpose, and says plainly that the original is obscure but he cannot see these things in it; he prefers a version followed by almost all the older translations, in which those who oppose God seize unjustly upon his cities, and applies it to the enemies who tried to drive the returned exiles out of the land. Ellicott calls the state of the text unsatisfactory on the same ground, that rendering enemies a word which properly means cities is very doubtful, though one Greek translator gives rivals and another adversaries; for the first clause he adopts a change of the vowel pointing that yields who rebel against thee, and for the second the simplest of the proposed emendations. John Gill takes a different tack, noting that the word for the wicked is singular in the original and reporting one Jewish commentator who referred it to Esau and so, in the rabbinic idiom, to the Christians.

On the hatred itself they part sharply. John Wesley disposes of it in a line, telling the reader to see the difference between the Jewish and the Christian spirit. Gill and Clarke both narrow it instead: Gill says good men hate the wicked not as men and creatures of God, whom the Gospel teaches them to love and pray for, but as haters of God, and their works rather than their persons; Clarke says he holds their conduct in abomination and abhors their motives and purposes. Ellicott renders it as a question, must I not hate thy haters, and compares a phrase of Tennyson about being dowered with the hate of hate. Clarke then makes the sharpest observation in the chapter: the psalmist needed to offer the closing prayer precisely because he had just uttered the imprecation, since he who utterly hates the practices of any man is not far from hating the man himself. Keil and Delitzsch note the turn that the searching confessed in the first verse has become a searching entreated, and Clarke and Ellicott agree that the way asked for at the end is the old way.
